utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Djordjevic, if I'm well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Djordjevic into the courtroom. I take the opportunity since the witness is not there yet, Mr. Josse, I take it that you're aware that at least in relation to Foca that there are a lot of adjudicated facts ranging from number 327 up till and including - there are hundreds of them - 608. Almost 300 facts already established in relation to Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you're called to testify in this court. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give your testimony, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, please proceed. Examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Slavko Djordjevic, and you were born in the Foca municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have lived there for many, many years, and you worked in the hospital as the head -- as a medical technician; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, I think, presently you still work there as the head medical technician in the surgery department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the head technician at the surgery department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right that you lived in 1990, shall we say, in Foca town itself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right that that was a town that at that time was split almost -- well, roughly 50 per cent Serb population, 50 per cent Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the total population of the town was about 15.000 inhabitants at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the town itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the total number of inhabitants in the municipality of Foca was about 40.000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, isn't this all in the adjudicated facts, 327, according to the 1991, it says that Foca municipality had a population of so and so much people? We are going over ground which is already in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll certainly move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with your background, you were a member of the Communist Party between 1974 and 1978; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a deputy in the BiH Congress as a representative of the health authority of Foca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I just say something? I was the representative of the health industry between 1974 and 1978, and I was a member of the League of Communists until it fell apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you. It's my fault. You were a member of the League of Communists until 1990 and the 1974 to 1978 was when you were a representative of the Congress. That's right, isn't it? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you joined the SDS in 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, recently you have become a deputy on behalf of the SDS in the Foca Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After the elections, I became a member of the SDS Board in Foca. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which elections were those, are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Recently in Foca, due to the fact that one member of the SDS stopped with his activities, new elections had to be held in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move back, if I may, to November 1990, and I want to ask you about a meeting that you attended at the football stadium in Foca, which was an SDS meeting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many people were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There should have been some 10.000 people at that rally at the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you just one of the 10.000 or did you take some active part in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a mere participant. I just attended the meeting, that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same year, 1990, tensions rose in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about television broadcasts and how they affected the tension.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we watched TV all the time, and there was some sort of a voting in the Assembly or delegates from Foca were present there. One of them was Saja Sainpasic. He was at the Assembly, and he said something that we didn't like. Actually, he sang something like "there's a duck, there's a goose, and this country will be Turkey." And already then at that time he already announced some tensions between the Serbs and the Muslims. This is what we watched on TV, and we did not care for that too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how -- in terms of weapons, were you aware of anyone being armed, so making the tension rise?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That started later on, on the eve of the war in 1992, at the beginning of that year that is. I saw with my two own eyes how my neighbour Saja got armed. I was standing at my window, and I saw him distributing some 40 rifles to his neighbours in the evening, and then they would stand duty with those rifles. All of these rifles had been in his garage. That was the beginning at 1992, during those months of the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Again, we'll come to that in a moment. Before we do that, I want to ask you about an incident at the Focatrans, which is a public transport enterprise in Foca.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is an incident in March of 1990.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it an incident that you're about to describe that again caused unrest and a rise in the feelings of the population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to elaborate a little. Focatrans was a public company for transport, and it employed both Serbs and Muslims. The head of the company was a Muslim. Because of some discourse some Serbs were fired, and after that there was some sort of a demonstration in front of the municipal building and in front of the Politika. The demonstrations lasted for two days and all of a sudden the Muslims disappeared from the rally. Nobody but the Serbs rallied. In order to calm down the Serbs, the specials were called from various parts, from Sarajevo. At their head was somebody called the Vikic who was the head of the special group belong to go Alija during the war. It was then when the Serb people in the Foca were beaten up, dispelled, and the Serbs were demoralised. They were angry. We didn't know why we were beaten. The demonstration was peaceful, and we didn't want anything but justice in our company. This was one of the tensions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you as well about the first meeting of the SDA in Foca. Did you witness that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA meeting took place in Pijesak on the right bank of the Drina some 50 metres away from my apartment. This is the area which is the size of two football pitches, an area by the Drina River. There was so many people there, as many as two stadiums could hold. I don't know how many there were. And it doesn't really matter that the meeting was held but that the Serbs were provoked from that meeting. A lot of people spoke at that meeting. Some Serbs attended the SDA meeting. I was on the edge of the football pitch, and I listened to all the discussions, and it was all good and well until people started moving through Foca in cars with two fingers in the air, with some flags, emblems, shouting provocations, and this is what we did not like, and this is one of the ways tensions were being created in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to follow that up in two or three ways. First of all, there's a map that we have of Foca town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one coloured copy and I think we've got two black and white copies. Perhaps the coloured one could go on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher will assist in putting it on the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'd like to you point out - you're going to be given a rod in which to do this pointing - where the Pijesak stadium on the right bank of the Drina is on that map.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Drina. This is Cehotina, this is the centre of town. This is Donje Polje where the majority of the population were Muslims. This is the detention centre about which I'm going to speak later on, and this is Pijesak. Here is Pijesak. Here is Pijesak. This is where I'm pointing to by the Drina River. This is a very large area called Pijesak. I just wanted to explain how the -- the map is actually drawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will take you through the various place you've pointed out at great speed a little slower as you go through your evidence. I think you showed where Pijesak is on the bank of the Drina. The next question I want to ask you is the flags that were being waved as the people went through the town, what sort of a flag --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, whenever a witness points at something, at a map, in order to avoid that anyone reading the testimony later has to consult the video, could you please briefly describe from -- if I would do it, I would say the witness pointed at what seems to be an area just north of where the two rivers come together immediately next to the river in green.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It would help if the map was back on the screen, please. It's not on my screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you take the other -- if you take the computer monitor button then you'll get it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I'd agree with Your Honour's description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put the --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since I live in Foca, I claim that the area that I am pointing to now, this area called Pijesak, was all covered by people during the SDS -- by the rally itself there are two buildings by the road. Everything else is just the area of -- called Pijesak and the village green called "the pitch." That's the name that it is known by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to answer to the questions but not to give any further information unless specifically asked. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Josse would like to have more details, he'll certainly ask for it. If not, he might have a lot of other questions for you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the answer that you just gave, Mr. Djordjevic, you said that it was during the SDS rally. I take it that was a slip of the tongue and you meant the SDA rally.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You described flags and emblems being waved in a provocative manner. What sort of flags and emblems were being waved in a provocative manner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were green flags and they raised two fingers through the car windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you take the two-fingered gesture to mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The two-fingered gesture is for Muslims, and the three-fingered gesture is the Serbian sign. And flashing either two or three fingers to each other is sort of an insult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that they were shouting slogans. What sort of slogans were they shouting as they were parading through Foca town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Various slogans. "This is going to be our country." "This is going to be a Muslim country." "You will have to move." Those things that our citizens listened to and felt provoked. Nothing could be done because these people were moving in the cars rather fast. They were waving those flags and showing two fingers in the air, and those were all provocations against the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I now want to move on to what you were in fact telling us before, namely the arming of persons in Foca. This begun, I think you told us, in the spring of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described witnessing this from your kitchen window?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you told us what you saw, and I don't think you need to go through that again. As a result of what you saw, rifles being distributed, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When the population saw that the Muslims were being armed, we also start asking for weapons. As soon as the arms were distributed amongst them, I personally got a rifle. We had in Foca the JNA, and towards the exit to -- from Foca towards Godjen we had a military hangar where there were weapons and, as far as I understand. I was not present there. We were also given weapons from those depots. Who distributed weapons I can't tell you. I don't have any proof. But I know that two lads, one called Tomovic and another called Mandic brought a rifle to me. I never used this rifle. I was a medical professional. I keep the rifle in the house and I never used it. That's how people were armed from various sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if I would read from the adjudicated facts that in the month before the outbreak of conflict in Foca and --"both Serbs and Muslims began to arm themselves with light weapons, though Muslims were is not able to do as quickly as the Serbs leaving the latter better prepared for the conflict." The first part of this sentence seems to be something which you are now establishing again it seems, or is there any specific detail --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness needs to describe this in outline in order for the rest of his testimony to make some sort of sense. I mean, could I take the whole of the evidence in absolute fragments, and I could perhaps -- I'm leading rather more than I have in the past. I could lead it more still. I'm more than happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be clear for the Chamber whether you're heading for presenting evidence which would -- which would challenge the adjudicated facts or whether -- because, if not -- of course, it could be that you say the personal observation is important for the Chamber to know in view of the evidence still to come, but arming Muslims and Serbs is something which is there already unless to be challenged, of course. But I did not get the impression that that was what you were aiming at. I just draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, quite the opposite. I mean, the witness -- as Your Honour rightly observed, the witness has accepted the adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You noticed that perhaps before. I was a bit cautious in saying these kind of things, but let's just -- again, if these personal observations are needed to establish the evidence still to be given, we have to accept that. At the same time, I draw your attention to not going over ground again which is already covered by adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be more a matter for Mr. Stewart than I, but ultimately unless we endeavour to, for example, adduce some evidence using 89(F), for the witness's evidence to make any sense he needs to go through, in my submission, the stages, albeit in outline, because what he's describing - what I'm attempting to get him to describe anyway - is the rise in tensions leading to the war in this particular municipality. If he doesn't mention the fact that both sides were armed, then it will make no sense all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want to make a big issue of this, but it seems to me when -- and, in future, when the opportunity is presented to either side to outline what they're trying to elicit from the witness or where they're trying to go, it may be prudent to decide whether that be done outside the presence of witness. As I say, in this instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'm a bit to be blamed for that as well. Well, please proceed, Mr. Josse. Let's see how it happens, but also if you look at 333 on the adjudicated facts, then you'd see "the tension are such --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd be lying if I said I had them in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of what Mr. Tieger just said, it might not be a good idea. Let's -- have you consulted them recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have not consulted them as recently as I should have done. I have read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then take that you -- that at least the relevant portion is available to you certainly during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll see to that. Could Your Honour give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I endeavour to have them before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically now about the hospital and what happened there in March of 1992. People -- the hospital up until that point was operating as a normal hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point individuals started taking refuge in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, who were the people that took refuge in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the hospital is rather large. It could accommodate 520 people with a lot of rooms. Every employee, including myself, on the eve of the war brought their family. I was in the hospital all the time. All the medical professionals of both Serb and Muslim ethnicity did the same without any problems. This is where they stayed until the moment they left the hospital as -- somewhat later on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about in Foca town itself? Was there population movement at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When war broke out on the 8th of April, already on the 9th of April, quite a few Muslims arrived at Foca hospital. Not because they had no where else to go in town but because they were afraid of war, and they wanted to seek shelter. And corridors were crowded with Muslim children, the elderly, and even young people. And they stayed awhile within the hospital, I mean, up until the moment when Serb forces took Foca, and then they left the hospital premises overnight basically, because they were afraid of repercussions, although nobody exerted any pressure. Nobody asked them to leave or -- not a single person was actually mistreated or abused in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's not quite the answer to the question I asked. I asked you about Foca town itself. Forget the hospital. Did people start moving around Foca town from one area to another?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't quite understand that's what you were after. However, from Donje Polje where I used to live, well, there were more Muslims there than Serbs, and whoever could travel went to places where there were more Serbs, near the church, in Cerezluk there were mostly Serbs there. And from the centre, for example -- well, Muslim left Cerezluk and went to places where there were nor Muslims such as Donje Polje. They were looking for places where they would feel safer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about older people? Were they able to move?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mine was a six-storey building. Half of the residents were Muslims and half were Serbs. Only elderly men and women remained in that apartment building, and they waited for the war basically. All the rest left, and I went to the hospital where I worked, and I actually never left the hospital premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the morning of the 7th of April of 1992 and what you encountered on the roads as you were returning to work.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The last day of my stay there was on the 7th. When I got up in the morning I saw a huge lorry in front of my apartment building, and it was parked sideways across the road, and that was where the first barricade was. So I was on my own, and I called my colleague, Zuko Sehka, or Suho, who was a Muslim woman and who was a good friend of mine. And I said to her, "Look, there is a barricade and I can't get through." And then I left the building and I went to the KP Dom to the penitentiary, that is, and there was a new barricade there, and my colleague Uzunovic Enes, who was a reserve police officer, was there and I was let through. There were no problems. I had no troubles, but on that occasion there were two barricades in Foca early in the morning. But during the day there were no barricades at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- well, I'm sure I can lead on this. It's right that your father died on the night of the 7th, morning of the 8th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right that you in fact buried him on the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was at the hospital when the hospital manager informed me that my father had died. Since there were barricades, I was unable to get there. I donned my white coat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And together with a number of other colleagues we were all wearing our white coats and we set off in the direction of a village called Bogavici which is near Cehotina, 17 kilometres away from Foca. I came across --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Show the learned Judges where that is on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Once again, this is Foca. This is the river Drina and this is Cehotina. Next to Cehotina you travel for about 17 kilometres. This is my place of birth, my family home, et cetera. So between Preljuca and Foca in the direction of Bogavici, the village of Bogavici. It figures in some maps but it doesn't seem to be on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got a map of the whole municipality if that would help, again, a coloured one for the ELMO and black and white one for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is already on one of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. This is, I hope, leading somewhere, Your Honour; that's why I'm pursuing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's right here, Foca. And Bogavici is here. It means that we came from the opposite direction. This is Bogavici. We came from Foca towards Slatina this way, and then we got here. Roughly speaking, 17 kilometres away, and it says "Bogovic" on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in order to get to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just for the record, Bogavici is quite in the north on this map, approximately in the middle of the northern boundary of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to get to Bogavici, what obstacles did you face?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At Godjen we came across barricade manned by armed Muslim reserve police officers. They knew me and they didn't say a word. They just said, "You can go through," because I was wearing my white coat. About five to six kilometres further, we came across two barricades. There was a huge trunk, a tree trunk, across the road. We moved it. And then there was a pile of rocks, and it was placed there by Muslim villagers. And there was nobody else there, and we just removed those rocks and got to the house safely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the return journey, was there any difficulty with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were even two Muslims who attended the funeral service at the cemetery, and on that occasion I saw and also my family who lived in the village told me about some kind of tension between the Serbs and the Muslims, and I went back to Foca with my colleagues at 6.00 and we went straight to the hospital. There were no barricades left on the roads. Everything had been removed. I entered the hospital at 6.00, and I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you continued working at the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the hospital that evening, the evening of the 8th of April, what did you see from the hospital was happening in parts of the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, upon my arrival at the hospital, at around 8.00 or 9.00, all of a sudden shooting started from all sides around Foca. Muslims kept -- or held the left bank called Siste, and Serbs held the right bank of the river called Celovina, and there was shooting coming from all sides. We had no casualties coming in that night, but from the surgical ward, from the terrace of the hospital, since it was on the fourth and the fifth floor, we could see the first fires, that is to say the houses that had been set on fire. And there was a great deal of shooting. We could hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go back to the plan, please, of Foca town. Where did you see the fires coming from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I can indicate it on the map. This is the hospital, and that's where we could see the fire, to the left of the hospital. From the first bridge and the hotel in the direction of Celovina in this area. And there are houses here near the forest, and it was where the last houses were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer to have north on top of the map and -- because it's a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So I should turn it around this way. That might be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would also like to know -- to find exactly where the hospital is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that was exactly my next question, precisely. That's why I was asking the witness to slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, and just answer the question, Mr. Djordjevic: Point out the hospital.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to do that with -- by coming around the map? That's much better. So looking at the map, towards the north on the river; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just after the river, after these flats here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point next to the centre of Foca town.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Between the mouth of the River Drina and Cehotina is the main town centre. There are two bridges here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the distance from the town centre to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Kilometre and a half, tops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now go back to the area, to the map, that particular orientation, in other words, north as far as we could see -- no, no. Don't change the maps. I'm sorry. Now point out again where you say you saw houses that were on fire.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed at an area immediately north of the northern of the two bridges, very close to that bridge on the right bank of the small river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the hospital, you gleaned information as to whose houses were alight?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We discovered that the first houses set on fire were Serb houses. I'm saying this on purpose because we were all anxious to find out whose houses were on fire. We were afraid it might be our houses. And when we saw the fires, somebody apparently had phoned that Zubar Kovacevic's, Drago Obrenovic's, and another person's, an electrician's house, whose name was on the list, was on fire. So, at any rate, four houses were set alight very close to the forest just after the bridge near Cehotina. That's the end of the suburban area, and those were the first houses set on fire in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would be able to name the persons to whom those houses belonged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how have you learnt that information?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you. I, too, wanted to find out whether my house was perhaps on fire because it was very close to that area and so we kept phoning around to our neighbours and we wanted to find out what was on fire in Foca. And it was very easy to get that information and we got it very fast. So it was Kovacevic's, Kovac's, Obrenovic's, and Drakula's house. So those four houses were on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said you saw gunfire. I'm not going to deal with that at the moment. It's right that the first wounded fighters began to arrive at the hospital on the 9th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also right and, broadly speaking, it's an adjudicated fact that it took about ten days for the Serbs to gain control of Foca town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal with the casualties who arrived at your hospital in those ten days. Was there any particular obvious ethnic bias in the casualties that arrived?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Foca, in a way, was rid of that sort of fighting within ten days. The first two or three days we had quite a few wounded, both Serbs and Muslims, and we couldn't tell who was who, and we -- we received them at the surgical ward. And I worked there. And they got exactly the same treatment. They shared rooms and there were no incidents, and my surgeons operated on more than 60 severely wounded patients both from the Serb and the Muslim side, and nobody died. And a couple of heavily injured Muslims were sent to a special clinic in Sarajevo. And there is all of that information on hospital -- in hospital files. So in as far as the surgical ward is concerned, what I'm telling you now is the truth. The patients stayed on the ward for a number of days until they recovered, and when they were recovered they were released from hospital. And afterwards, as far as I found out, some of those soldiers were also sent to the penitentiary, in fact, for questioning and were kept there. So that's as much as I have to say about the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, after the fighting has ended, you visited a place called Elektrodistribucija?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's a bigger company next to my apartment building. It's called Elektrodistribucija, and when the area was liberated, I was called by an electrician who wanted to give me some stuff for my home. And also, in the course of this fighting, my apartment was demolished and quite a few things were taken away and stolen, and so the electrician gave me back a pen, a fountain pen that I had, and it said my -- it had my name on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. You see, you're not answering my question. My question was a simple one, and I was going to develop your evidence on this a little more slowly and --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing I want to ascertain is during the fighting, this place, Elektrodistribucija, was used for a particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his purpose?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a surgery for the nursing of the wounds of the injured on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right, it was basically a field hospital for the Muslims during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a mini-surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you've already told us, when the fighting had stopped, you went there. It was very near your apartment, and you found some of your belongings there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had happened to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My flat was demolished and the rifle that had been given to me for my personal use is something that I had never used, and they took it away and they took some bedding. And I am a nurse, and I used to teach first aid, and I had a special first aid kit which was taken away as well. And some of my belongings I found again at that company, Elektrodistribucija, and I saw items which had the name of my family and my own name. Those were personal belongings that had been taken out of my flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness the Serbs gaining control of Foca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Within five to six days, yes. But for as long as I was at the hospital, nobody was allowed to move about or leave the hospital, so I couldn't visit any places or see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it became clear that the Serbs were going to establish control of the town, what happened to the Muslim staff in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Within 20 to 25 days the Muslim staff left the hospital. It was their own initiative. Nobody had been mistreated in any way. And following the orders of the then director, and I got a van and I took Dr. Kucuk, Dr. Asima, Dr. Tafro and took them to their flats because it was still rather safe. Nobody interfered with anyone else, especially in as far as the medical staff was concerned. Twenty days later I found that they had all crossed over to Yugoslavia with no problem at all. So that was about the medical staff. Some nurses had left, and this colleague of mine, Mrs. Zuka, that I mentioned before is living in Denmark today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did she leave? The hospital, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Straight after those doctors. I myself accompanied her to her flat and she boarded a bus together with all of her family and her two sons. First of all she went to Montenegro, and then from there she went to Denmark and that's where she's living at the moment. And I did the same to Gohdija Refija and Hamdo. And Hamdo is working at the orthopaedic hospital in Sarajevo. He used to work at the surgical ward. I took him to his flat and finally he went to Montenegro. And today he's living in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those ten days, did you witness any discrimination in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I claim upon my full responsibility that there wasn't any discrimination. It was our task as medical staff, and it is a task for medical staff everywhere in the world to take equal care of all our patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Muslim staff left, did they take any supplies or medication with them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Those who left at that stage, no. But there's also other information that in the course of the preparations for the war they did take some stuff. Do you want me to elaborate that point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the head nurse, the chief nurse, and I realised that I was short of some bandages and certain medication. Armina Kunavac [phoen] would take as much as a hundred metres of bandages home and my nurses told me about that. And then Emina Basic, after the end of the war, was found in the possession of 25 kilogrammes of cotton wads. And somebody called Mandzo who was a nurse as well had 100 ammonia capsules. And we afterwards realised through some experts that it was intended for poisoning the water supplies. So those are just some examples. So I've given you these names. And there was evidence to support that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when these items were taken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The war started on the 8th, so this could have been sometime in March, in the month of March. Those were the preparations for the surgeries, for treating people during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as we've got to the point where the war had started, after the Serbs had gained control of Foca, what happened to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The hospital continued operating. It still works with its full capacity. We still have Muslim patients. And at that time the hospital only treated -- only worked with the Serbs because the Muslims had left. Currently we don't have any Muslim staff because nobody wanted to be employed at the hospital. There are no returnees with that profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking, literally, about currently right now, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think you're jumping ahead a little bit. I'm trying to deal with 1992 and what happened after the Serbs took control of Foca. So that's what I want you to concentrate on, please, Mr. Djordjevic. The hospital continued to function. You, I think, have told us that there were still some Muslim patients; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You continued to work at the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We treated them as everybody else. And then for safety reasons, for their sake, we took a van. We took two or three wounded children --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the question was whether you continued to work at the hospital. Tell us if you were, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. I'm sorry, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the hospital -- I'm going to rephrase that if I may. At some point in 1992, you started working in places other than the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of those places that you worked in was the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, as you've already told us, was a prison that was in Foca.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point it out, please, on the map.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's -- is that the large red building that we see in the middle of the map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's close to the bridge which is north of the town of Foca over the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often or how many times in 1992 did you visit the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I went there a dozen times or so to dress the wounds of those patients who had been treated at the surgery department. We just continued their treatment at the KP Dom. I was sent there as an experienced nurse to administer drugs to them and dress their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware, certainly now, of 462 through Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to -- many, many numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The situation at the KP Dom takes a large portion of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I still intend to adduce this evidence, with Your Honour's leave. Clearly the Court needs to hear what it is first of all. It's -- I won't comment upon it. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I do understand. Mr. Josse, I think the case law of this Tribunal is that adjudicated facts, of course, can be challenged, but they're accepted only if in two instances -- or at least if they're established after adjudication, not on -- on the basis of guilty pleas. It -- I mean, just from -- let me just say from what I saw from the 65 ter summary which was -- if you look at the last sentence, it is put in a negative formula which certainly would not be something to -- to support challenging the adjudicated the facts. I'm not denying any right of the Defence to -- I would say to take a frontal attack, but of course it would need more than what we see at this moment in the 65 ter summary. I'm expressing myself in this way in order not to influence in whatever way the witness. So therefore I'll take it you'll keep this clearly in the back of your mind if you start questioning about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again - I'm sure I can deal with this reasonably cryptically - I expect the witness to say what is contained in that document, the document Your Honour has referred to; no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would take us not more than three minutes, would I say, so just to have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djordjevic, you went to the KP Dom. I think I was asking you on how many occasions. You may have said, through 1992. It was about ten; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went there for specific purposes on those ten occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose that you were asked to go to the prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My friend Alija Beboric -- actually, Amir Berberkic was in prison. He was a surgeon who was in the front line. He was brought to the surgery department wounded. We treated them and he was discharged from the hospital to the KP Dom for further observation and I interviews I suppose. I went to dress his wounds there. There were no problems. He was not at any risk, and I also dressed the wounds of all the other people who were wounded. I also found my friend and colleague Amir Suzanic [phoen] who had been on the barricades, and he was also at the KP Dom at the time. In other words, I was sent there to administer drugs to those who suffered any pain and to dress their wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the Chamber might be interested in this: When you administered these drugs or tended to the wounds of these prisoners, where did you do that? Whereabouts in the prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The rooms in the prison are large. In each of them there is some 20 people. Those rooms would be open for me. Would I go in. I would tend to the wounds. I had my medical supplies on me. I didn't have any problems. People were grateful to me. They don't -- didn't complain of anything to me. In other words, it was there on the spot in the rooms where I tended to the wounded and to the patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's no dispute about this. At -- during the war the KP Dom was used as a detention facility for Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I perhaps should ask you this follow-up question: Are you able to say, from anything you saw or heard, the type of Muslims that were detained at the KP Dom? Let me be more specific, soldiers, civilians, anything along those lines?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see a single woman or a single child. They were all middle-aged men ranging from my age down to younger. None of them wore a military uniform. They -- some of them wore the uniform of the reserve police, and most of those people had participated in war activities. Amir Beberkic was in civilian clothes but he had been in the war. When the conflict broke out, 90 per cent of the population did not have any uniforms. So it was very difficult for me to tell whether they were civilians or whether they were members of the military. In any case, they were all able-bodied men, in my view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic that I think we can deal with shortly. After the Serbs had taken control of Foca, there was no more fighting in the town itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were therefore able to walk around the town freely?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your either understanding or what did you see or hear in relation to the Muslim population after the Serbs took control?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question fully. If you're referring to the population, I can say that isn't Serbs took over the population left the town. When I told you that people left the hospital, I meant that as soon as we could move freely about the town there were no longer any Muslims there. Maybe an odd one here and there in their apartments, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to how and why the Muslims left the town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: For safety reasons. No patient died at the surgery department. I never saw a dead Muslim or Serb fighter at the surgery department after the war operations. Later on, seven Serb soldiers died. We all treated them at the hospital. I didn't see any fighting in the town because we never left the hospital. And as for the population, in the course of two or three days when the Serbian soldiers took over Foca, they had to leave Foca of their own will. They were not expelled. They left the town for their own safety. For safety reasons, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could I just put one follow-up question. You said "for safety reasons." To what extent they were unsafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Muslims were in Donje Polje and when they were -- when they had prevalence there, they incarcerated all the Serbs in the KP Dom. And when the Serbs took over, the Muslims had to leave for fear of retaliation. And if the Muslims had been found by the Serbs, I'm sure that the Serbs would have retaliated against them. This was also true before the war. Wherever there were more Muslims, Muslims would go there. And I'm sure that there would have been more casualties if the Muslims had waited for the Serbs in the town. They had to leave for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you consider their fear realistic once the Serbs had taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to request that the Court take a 40-minute break now. I frankly -- I've got one other topic that I wish to deal with. I need to speak to Mr. Krajisnik. He raised one particular matter as he came into court in relation to this witness I need to discuss with him. I say I suspect I won't be very much longer. So 40 minutes would be very useful to me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, usually I'm stealing some of the minutes. Let me be generous once. We will adjourn and resume at a quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I take it that you had an opportunity to communicate with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, and that's really why I asked -- I've asked the witness to remain out of court because there's a matter that I think perhaps I should introduce and Mr. Tieger may understandably wish to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The history, it won't take me very long to go through it. On Friday, I think, of last week, I had a brief meeting with Mr. Krajisnik at the UNDU. It was rather curtailed. In it he handed over some documents in relation to both Mr. Stavnjak and Mr. Djordjevic. As Your Honour may know, I was then -- I was basically away for four days. I personally didn't take the documents with me. There was absolutely no point. I handed them over to the interpreter who was with me, and for my part, frankly, forgot about them until shortly little before Your Honours came in to court at about 2.15 today when I was reminded of them. Mr. Krajisnik is anxious that I put them to the witness. Your Honours had better see them. They are newspaper articles, in fact, and there are two extracts. The relevant parts have been translated by our team, but at least that's something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's something, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could I put them into context, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They are interviews on two different dates. I'm not sure. It may be I think in two different newspapers with the same man, a man called Halid Cengic. One, we can see was in 1997. The other was in 1998. And they deal with effectively covert arming of Muslims before the war, and Mr. Krajisnik is anxious that I introduce these in effect as evidence via the witness to establish that there was covert arming, and in particular he says, and I'd submit that this is right, that that has some bearing on the testimony of the last witness and what happened in Gorazde and how the Muslims there were armed. Now, Your Honour, I have recognised that I have literally only just served these on Mr. Tieger. To some extent, in fairness, that wasn't Mr. Krajisnik's fault for the reasons I have already explained. I hope Mr. Krajisnik will forgive me for putting it this way. I also appreciate that, notwithstanding the adjudicated facts, let's leave them to one side, they're not going to take this case very much further. Nonetheless, it's my submission that I should be allowed to ask the witness, first of all, if he knows who Mr. Cengic is, then to ask him about these two different passages and whether he can comment upon them. I hope that adequately explains the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first here what Mr. Tieger would like to say in response to -- and then I also see that apart from the two newspaper articles I also find a list of some 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Don't worry about that, Your Honour. That will only arise if the witness answers another question I've been asked to ask in a particular way. That, I think, there can be no possible objection to. It's an OTP document as we can see from the number and it doesn't need translating. I can't see how that would have any objection to that. In fact it may not arise at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful to my learned friend for anticipating my reaction both at the moment he gave me these documents a moment before we resumed court and once court began. The point is not either the -- at this moment, the relevance of the substantive material to the issues at hand or even the extent to which that relevance may have been obviated by the adjudicated facts, which is an issue the court alluded to and which counsel alluded to. The fact is I just got those. I know the translations are short but the articles are significantly longer insofar as I can tell, and I don't have any idea, of course, what they say, and so it's quite predictable that I have no choice but to object. Now, whether or not there's a solution the Court can craft which satisfies what counsel has acknowledged as my understandable concerns and the need to move forward as expeditiously as possible. I don't know. But of course under these circumstances I'm not prepared to deal with these documents appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I perhaps first ask a question. Mr. Krajisnik, I'll give you an opportunity in a second. Ljiljan, what kind of a periodical is that? I mean -- let me just -- it would -- might make a difference when it was a party newspaper for any political party or -- I don't remember that I've ever come across that name before, but I might -- might be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is a Muslim newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A Muslim newspaper, is the description I've been given of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a Muslim newspaper. Of course, Oslobodjenje is sufficiently known.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Apparently it's for sale in this country at the moment. One could buy a copy, I'm told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in the Netherlands at the moment if one chose to. So I've been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I usually limit myself to Dutch newspapers at the newsstand but I should have a better look at it next time. Let me see. This is from 1998. They're both articles from 1998, from what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought one was 1997. The very end of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It says 31/12/1997 until the 3rd of January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the edition that bridges the new year of that -- of those two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed at that Mr. Krajisnik would like to say something about it. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to make two points, Your Honour. Yesterday, I received the documents from the Prosecution for the first time yesterday, and it was in English, and I didn't even ask for many explanations, and I would have been able to help my Defence team. And I would really like to appeal to the Prosecution not to object to these articles because we're talking about small parts of articles. And secondly, it is an interview given by their important figure. And this witness is in a position it shed more light on these facts in order for us to gain a complete picture of the -- of the overall situation in Foca at the time without wishing to shift the blame or anything, just to shed more light. And these are two excerpts, two short bits of text from an interview with this very important figure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder, but that's a general problem why we would need the newspapers to -- if the witness has any knowledge about, it we could ask him about it, isn't it? So therefore I would first -- and, of course, if the one who gives the interview has important information on the matter, of course one could consider to call that person or I don't know whether it's on your list of witnesses, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm sure this gentleman isn't, and I'm sure there's very little prospect of the Defence calling him, being realistic. The -- Your Honour, very helpfully, I think last week, it may have been the week before, tried to assist me with some general observations about the admission of what, excuse the expression, I might call slightly tenuous pieces of evidence being admitted through a particular witness. I suspect that's what -- that's what the Defence have in mind here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, I accept the link is relatively tenuous save for the fact that this is the Defence witness who is dealing with Foca. We're not planning, as far as I know, to call another witness in relation to Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I -- let me just have a look at what I've got in front of me. If I look at the Oslobodjenje, I do not see any single link with Foca in the part that was translated unless Ustikolina is in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is in the municipality, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in the municipality. It's at these -- then I take it that's -- then the other one starts with "Foca was the focal point," and the answer is, "I do not know if it was the focal point." That weakens the link with Foca, but let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the next sentence strengthens it, to be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not only -- but more as a -- I would say as a pivotal distribution centre than rather on the events in Foca itself. Let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber has decided that you should address the matter in the following way: Once the witness is back in court, you may examine the witness on the subject matter as we find it in the -- especially in the translated parts. Let's first wait and see what kind of answers we get on those questions, and you might be yourself in a position to see whether it makes any sense at all to introduce these documents in relation to this witness. Whether or not at another moment, when fully translated, there would be good reason to present them as contextual exhibits or something else is still to be seen, but let's first start without specific reference to the articles and then at the end that you first make up your mind as to whether it makes any sense to do it, and if you think it would, then ask permission to the Chamber and we will then consider whether or not we will allow you to confront the witness with these articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say two things in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Firstly, I understand that at some point, certainly not in my presence, they have been shown to the witness. So he may have some knowledge of them -- of the matters because he's seen the articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just if the Chamber would bear that in mind when I ask the questions. Secondly, at any rate, before he saw the articles I was going to ask him what knowledge he had of Halid Cengic. Perhaps I could do that in any event as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps you be very precise in asking for the factual basis on which he answers the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because, finally, the factual basis would be that he read all about it in newspaper articles then, of course, it's -- then we are turning around in circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then, Mr. Tieger, I -- Mr. Josse has had an opportunity to briefly add a few meant to what the Chamber just said. If there would be any need from your part, I would give you an opportunity. If not, I'll ask the witness to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, there's no need, Your Honour. Thank you, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I want to ask you a few other matters, please. First of all, do you know where Ustikolina is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the map of Foca - perhaps that could be put back on the ELMO - would you point it out to the Chamber. It's --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Down the River Drina 12 kilometres away from here. About 12 kilometres away from Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, if you go a bit more up north from Foca. A little bit more up even. Up, up, up. Up, up, up. I think you're close to a place which is now indicated a little bit to the left where at least the map says it's Ustikolina. And for the record --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ustikolina is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's full north from the town much Foca at approximately 80 per cent to the north of a municipality border. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any Muslim units having been formed there in 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is this: Do you know -- does the name Halid Cengic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It rings a bell. I think he was a Municipal Councillor. He was a neighbour from Ustikolina but I didn't know him in person. I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the arming of Muslims, you gave earlier in your testimony some personal recollections of witnessing a particular arming incident from your window where you lived. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being more general, do you have any other knowledge, just answer this yes or no, please, of arming of Muslims prior to the war in --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Listen carefully to my question. Where does that knowledge come from, something you've seen, something you've heard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a colleague of mine at the surgical ward, Enes Uzunovic who asked me to allow him to attend meetings of reserve police officers, and he actually went off duty on those occasions. And later on other citizens could see it. They would -- I mean, these people would go to the meetings and they would not be armed but they would come back armed with an automatic rifle or something like that. So this was the way in which they were arming people at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any knowledge of widespread arming?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. If I may point out, this was done sporadically. People were trying to make do, and they would sometimes get arms. But as to any large-scale arming operations in the area of Foca, I know nothing about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question in this regard. Do you know anything about arming of Muslims that concerned Senad Safirpasic who you mentioned certainly year as the person who had pronounced a rather ugly slogan who I think was also known as Sadja? First of all, do you know who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Senad Sainpasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know who I'm talk about, it's my pronunciation. Do you remember earlier you told us about someone you had seen on the television saying something along the line duck is swimming, goose is swimming, this land shall be Turkish?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the person who said that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sainpasic, Saja, who was distributing weapons from across where I lived. But he was a councillor at the Assembly, and he made up those verses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll take this in stages. He had a nickname which was Saja, I think you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Saja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse my mispronunciation. Saja. You then begun to tell us about his involvement with the distribution of weapons. Where does your knowledge of this man's distribution of weapons come from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't actually have any knowledge, anything more than I saw. I could see how he was distributing those weapons. But as to who gave the weapons to him or anything else, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is my fault. The person you saw distributing the weapons was a person, Saja, who had also -- Saja, beg your pardon, who had also pronounced this very ugly slogan that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in my submission there is a link so far as the 1998 article is concerned, the May one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that it at least gives some support, although the knowledge of the witness seems not to be very extensive, then nevertheless there's certainly a link which could be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And obviously I'll seek to develop it once the witness has seen the document if the Court gives leave for him to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before we do so, I'd then like to ask one. You told us that you saw Saja distributing arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us that you do not know who gave the arms to him, that you had no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that was done in secret. We had no idea. We saw the weapons when people displayed them, showed them. I suppose that the Serbs got the weapons from the JNA. And as to where the Muslims got them from, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even a clue? Did you ever hear about from whom he got them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Never read anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never read anything at all about it, no articles. I just have no idea where they got the weapons from. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that true for Foca only or also wider for Bosnia and Herzegovina, or do you have any idea on how Muslims, if they were arming themselves, how they would distribute their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. Normal citizens had no way of knowing or finding out. We didn't know how it was done. I was given a rifle by some young man, and I didn't even ask him where he got it. I just felt that it was a welcome gift and that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I would like to ask you to leave the courtroom just for a couple of minutes, because we'd like to discuss a procedural matter which we'd prefer to discuss in your absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, there are several options. You confront the witness with the newspaper article on a matter which without a newspaper article he says he doesn't know anything about it. Another option would be to have the newspaper article fully translated so that we have the full of the context here, that you tender it into evidence, because I can't imagine that many the Defence takes the position that at least the testimony of Saja distributing weapons is supported by this newspaper article to the extent that someone else refers to Saja as inviting weapons to be taken into his house, which of course could be logically understood that someone who, with weapons in his house, is in a position to distribute them. So therefore it would certainly add, I would say, to the credibility and reliability in respect of the testimony. I would like to give you an opportunity to say what you'd prefer and what you think is fair to do at this moment apart from the other article. I have not spoken about that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to say my client is in agreement with the submission I was going make which was the latter course that Your Honour was suggesting. Perhaps I could make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The list, that you have it translated and tender it in evidence, and then hear from the Prosecution whether they would object in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. And perhaps I can make this comment, as much as anything, for Mr. Krajisnik's benefit bearing in mind I'm unable to speak to him now. The fact that the witness, of course, hasn't seen the article, doesn't know anything about it, very much -- I appreciate this is a comment, but very much supports his testimony. If he was saying my testimony relies on the article, then it would -- it might impugns his credibility, but he's saying the two are completely separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least Saja distributing weapons within the sight of the witness most likely is not taken from any newspaper article. That's what is clear. May I take it that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the article will share the same fate as this one, waiting for translation and to see whether it will be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it there's hardly anything from your side to be added to it. You might prepare for how to respond to tendering these newspaper articles in evidence, but we could leave it up to that moment, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's hard to imagine, Your Honour, how could I object to the forthcoming submission before it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you can't even read the articles. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Josse will continue his examination. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to briefly go back and deal with one other subject that I asked you about, and that was your visit to the KP Dom. Who sent you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My manager told me that in the absence of the doctors who were very busy that I should go to the KP Dom to tend to some wounds and to help there as much as I could. It was the director of the hospital who told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you any idea who was telling the director of the hospital that someone needed to go to the KP Dom, some medical person needed to go?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the director? It was Stanic Sekulic. I didn't understand the question.
